groups.label: Newton’s laws: statements, qualitative reasoning and interactions
groups.summary: Recognise what a force law says, which objects interact and what a resultant implies.

groups.label: Free-body diagrams, resultants and equilibrium
groups.summary: Build and resolve the real-force account before choosing a dynamics equation.

groups.label: Single-body linear dynamics
groups.summary: Distinguish resultant, named interaction and motion-derived acceleration.

groups.label: Connected bodies and internal forces
groups.summary: Choose a whole system for acceleration and the appropriate subsystem for an internal force.

groups.label: Surface friction
groups.summary: Distinguish the required static force, its maximum and the sliding law.

groups.label: Elastic restoring forces
groups.summary: Use extension relative to natural length and distinguish force from energy or oscillation.

groups.label: Pressure forces and buoyancy
groups.summary: Distinguish displaced-fluid density and volume from those of the object.

groups.label: Drag and terminal motion
groups.summary: Use drag direction, speed dependence and the correct limiting force balance.

groups.label: Momentum and system boundaries
groups.summary: Construct the momentum vector and decide whether a stated system can conserve it.

groups.label: Impulse and impacts
groups.summary: Use signed/vector momentum change and distinguish average net force from a contact force.

groups.label: Collisions and their energy consequences
groups.summary: Keep the momentum balance, collision constraint and energy test separate.

groups.label: Explosions, recoil and separation
groups.summary: Model internal separation, reference velocities and released energy.

groups.label: Momentum flow and changing-mass situations
groups.summary: Find force from momentum crossing a boundary rather than blindly applying a fixed-mass equation.

groups.label: Circular-motion quantities and concepts
groups.summary: Distinguish speed, angular speed, radial acceleration and the work done by different forces.

groups.label: Horizontal circular-force arrangements
groups.summary: Identify the real inward force while satisfying independent vertical balance.

groups.label: Vertical circles and loss of contact
groups.summary: Write the radial force equation at the named location and impose the physical contact condition.

groups.label: Field forces in a mechanics problem
groups.summary: Separate an A.2 force/momentum step from the field-specific knowledge supplying it.

groups.label: Experimental tests and representations of mechanics
groups.summary: Keep physical-model inference separate from generic plotting and uncertainty operations.

Third law: interaction pairs and their consequences

Rebuild the force account after a change

Use kinetic friction and infer its parameters
Combine elastic force with other forces
Distinguish conserved momentum from kinetic energy

types.label: State Newton’s first law
types.summary: Explicit request for the first-law statement, rather than a numerical balance.
checks: State both rest/constant-velocity possibilities and the condition of zero net external force.
types.boundary_note: A force-balance calculation is a separate equilibrium leaf.

types.label: Explain an inertia effect when support or vehicle motion changes
types.summary: An unrestrained object appears to lag, continue or move relative to a vehicle.
checks: Describe motion in an inertial frame; distinguish lack of a new force from a force of motion.
types.boundary_note: Explicit transformations and inertial-frame theory primarily belong to A.5.

types.label: Define or recognise an inertial reference frame
types.summary: The actual demand is to define or select a reference frame.
checks: An inertial frame is non-accelerating; Newton’s laws retain their form.
types.boundary_note: A.5 HL demand using A.2 knowledge; supporting only in the A.2 question census.

types.label: Apply the zero-resultant / constant-velocity condition
types.summary: Infer what zero resultant or constant velocity implies, without solving a force balance.
checks: Use the equivalence of zero resultant and constant velocity in an inertial frame.
types.boundary_note: Calculating unknown balancing forces belongs in equilibrium; explicit zero-force/zero-acceleration selection belongs in qualitative second-law reasoning.

types.label: State or express Newton’s second law
types.summary: State the law or express the proportionality between resultant force and acceleration for fixed mass.
checks: Relate resultant force to mass and acceleration for constant mass.
types.boundary_note: Use momentum-law leaf when the rate of momentum change is the assessed point.

types.label: Define the newton through unit-mass acceleration
types.summary: The force unit or its mechanical definition is asked for.
checks: Connect 1 N with 1 kg accelerated at 1 m s−2.

types.label: Define inertial mass as resistance to acceleration
types.summary: The ratio of resultant force to acceleration or meaning of inertial mass is requested.
checks: Use m = Fnet/a and distinguish inertial mass from weight or amount of substance.

types.label: Distinguish velocity direction from resultant-force or acceleration direction
types.summary: A path, field line or sequence of positions is shown and directions of velocity and acceleration must be compared.
checks: Velocity is tangent to the trajectory; acceleration points with the resultant force, not necessarily with the velocity.
types.boundary_note: A.1 supplies path/velocity interpretation; a field context may also require D.1–D.3.

types.label: Judge whether force and mass give constant or changing acceleration
types.summary: Explain why acceleration changes, or when constant-acceleration equations are permitted.
checks: Compare F_net/m across the motion; do not confuse constant drive with constant resultant.
types.boundary_note: A calculation of the new acceleration remains under quantitative linear dynamics.

types.label: Explain qualitatively how a resultant changes motion
types.summary: Explain speeding up, slowing down or turning using force and acceleration.
checks: Identify resultant direction relative to velocity, then infer the change of motion.
types.boundary_note: Use specialised drag/circular leaves where the changing resistance or geometry is the main demand.

types.label: Relate net force to change of velocity, not velocity or change of speed
types.summary: Choose the quantity or vector direction tied to resultant force.
checks: Resultant force is parallel to acceleration, hence to the rate of change of velocity.
types.boundary_note: A speed can remain unchanged while the velocity vector changes.

types.label: Distinguish zero acceleration from zero speed, velocity or momentum
types.summary: Zero resultant is given; choose what must vanish.
checks: F_net = 0 implies a = 0, not necessarily v = 0 or p = 0.
types.boundary_note: No numerical substitution is needed.

types.label: State Newton’s third law
types.summary: A general statement of action and reaction is requested.
checks: Specify equal magnitude, opposite direction, same interaction and different bodies.

types.label: Identify a concrete Newton-third-law pair
types.summary: The other force in a specified interaction must be named or selected.
checks: Swap the agent and receiving body; keep the interaction, magnitude and line of action.
types.boundary_note: Weight and support acting on one body are not a third-law pair.

types.label: Compare interaction forces despite unequal masses or accelerations
types.summary: A heavy/light pair, collision or towing system tempts unequal action–reaction forces.
checks: Use equal-and-opposite interaction forces; then distinguish accelerations through different masses.

types.label: Explain why an interaction pair does not cancel on one body
types.summary: The question challenges how motion occurs when action and reaction are equal.
checks: Draw separate body boundaries; internal pairs cancel only in the combined-system resultant.

types.label: Apply the third law independently of masses and collision elasticity
types.summary: Test whether the third law applies to a stated interaction.
checks: The two bodies exert simultaneous, equal and opposite interaction forces.
types.boundary_note: Conservation of kinetic energy is not a condition for Newton’s third law.

types.label: Identify the physical agent or nature of a force
types.summary: A force’s source, contact/field nature, or physical origin is the demand.
checks: Name the two interacting bodies and the mechanism without inventing a force of motion.
types.boundary_note: Detailed microscopic models may belong to another topic.

types.label: Draw or select a complete real-force diagram
types.summary: Forces on one named object must be shown.
checks: Isolate that object; include each real interaction with a correct direction and label.
types.boundary_note: Do not add velocity, acceleration or an extra centripetal force. A contact force may be represented as one oblique resultant or as separate normal and friction components; never count both representations as extra forces.

types.label: Construct the force diagram on an incline
types.summary: The body contacts a sloping surface and may be pulled or sliding.
checks: Draw weight vertically, normal perpendicular to the surface and friction against relative slip.

types.label: Construct a fluid-force diagram before or during motion
types.summary: A submerged, falling, rising or terminal-speed body requires a diagram.
checks: Separate weight, buoyancy and drag; drag opposes motion and is zero at instantaneous rest in the stated model.

types.label: Construct a force diagram for circular motion
types.summary: A circular path tempts an outward arrow or an extra centripetal force.
checks: Draw real interactions; their inward resultant supplies the required radial acceleration.

types.label: Scale arrows to express equilibrium or a specified acceleration
types.summary: Correct force names are insufficient: relative arrow lengths decide the answer.
checks: Use the required resultant to compare force magnitudes on the chosen body.

types.label: Resolve a force into useful perpendicular components
types.summary: A force is angled to the horizontal, vertical or slope axes.
checks: Choose axes from the physical constraint; resolve with the angle measured from the correct axis.

types.label: Add or subtract force vectors to determine a resultant
types.summary: Find a resultant by signed collinear addition, a vector construction, or components.
checks: Use consistent directions/signs; add vectors. Resolve into components only when needed by the geometry.
types.boundary_note: An F = ma calculation using that resultant has a separate primary type. Vector addition does not automatically require trigonometric component resolution.

types.label: Recover a missing force by vector closure
types.summary: Find a missing force/equilibrant or recognise whether a head-to-tail force polygon closes.
checks: Use unknown force = required resultant minus the sum of known forces.
types.boundary_note: Recognising a closed triangle does not require solving component equations numerically.

types.label: Test possible magnitudes of a resultant
types.summary: Force magnitudes are known but relative directions may vary.
checks: Use geometric bounds and limiting parallel/antiparallel cases.
types.boundary_note: Do not confuse a range test with one fixed diagram.

types.label: Infer zero resultant from rest or constant velocity
types.summary: A body is at rest or travels with constant velocity under multiple forces.
checks: Set the vector sum of forces to zero; retain non-zero individual forces.

types.label: Test component equations for two-dimensional equilibrium
types.summary: A force diagram or equations must satisfy balance in two directions.
checks: Set both component sums to zero; do not infer balance from one axis alone.

types.label: Find tensions or angles for a statically supported load
types.summary: A load hangs from multiple strings or angled supports.
checks: Resolve each tension and impose horizontal and vertical equilibrium.

types.label: Find normal force when a push or pull has a vertical component
types.summary: An angled applied force changes the contact force without vertical acceleration.
checks: Balance forces normal to the surface before calculating friction.

types.label: Find the normal reaction on an incline
types.summary: The requested force is perpendicular to a sloping surface; no additional normal acceleration is present.
checks: Resolve weight perpendicular to the plane and include any other perpendicular force components; in the simple case N = mg cos θ.

types.label: Find force, mass or acceleration from a stated resultant
types.summary: The given force is explicitly net/resultant.
checks: Use ΣF = ma with consistent units and direction.

types.label: Find an unknown force or acceleration from several forces
types.summary: A driving force and one or more opposing forces are present.
checks: Construct the signed resultant first, then use ΣF = ma.

types.label: Compare accelerations or resultants when mass and force change
types.summary: Quantities change by factors rather than a complete set of initial numbers.
checks: Form a₂/a₁ = (Fnet,2/Fnet,1)(m₁/m₂); distinguish applied force from resultant.

types.label: Find acceleration on a smooth or otherwise specified incline
types.summary: Weight and applied forces must be resolved along a slope.
checks: Use slope-parallel ΣF = ma and independent perpendicular balance.

types.label: Find acceleration under an angled applied force
types.summary: A force pulls or pushes at a stated angle while motion is constrained to a line.
checks: Resolve the applied force along the permitted motion and apply ΣF∥ = ma; do not use its full magnitude.
types.boundary_note: Use the appropriate complementary angle when the angle is measured from the vertical.

types.label: Couple translational force balance to rolling dynamics
types.summary: A rolling body accelerates on a slope or under an applied force and rotational inertia cannot be ignored.
checks: Write ΣF = ma alongside τ = Iα and the no-slip constraint; identify the role and direction of static friction.
types.boundary_note: Mixed current A.4 HL. Pure rotational energy or inertia calculations are not A.2.

types.label: Infer force or mass from motion data
types.summary: Acceleration is not supplied directly but speeds, distance, time or a velocity graph are.
checks: Recover acceleration from the motion, then identify the resultant or named force.
types.boundary_note: Cross-topic with A.1; retain the actual force demand.

types.label: Carry a force-derived acceleration into speed, time or distance
types.summary: A force account is needed before a kinematics quantity can be found.
checks: Find acceleration from the resultant, then use the relevant motion relation.
types.boundary_note: Cross-topic with A.1.

types.label: Translate a force condition or history into a motion-related graph
types.summary: Force varies with time or position and the requested output is a motion representation.
checks: Use a = Fnet/m to determine signs, slopes and curvature; do not confuse force with speed.
types.boundary_note: Includes constant-force and changing-force cases. Use the requested axis variable; a kinetic-energy-time output is a mixed A.2/A.3 demand.

types.label: Connect driving force, speed and power in linear motion
types.summary: The target is a force but the available data are power and steady speed.
checks: Use P = Fv for the relevant parallel force, then apply force balance as required.
types.boundary_note: At constant force use average power = force times average speed; an energy/work route may avoid explicitly evaluating the force. A pure P = Fv substitution is A.3-primary context, not evidence that F = ma was used.

types.label: Predict engine power while acceleration is fixed and resistance changes
types.summary: A drive maintains constant acceleration against speed-dependent resistance; power versus time or speed is requested.
checks: Use Fdrive = ma + Fresist(v), then P = Fdrive v and the stated velocity-time relationship.
types.boundary_note: Mixed A.2/A.3; do not assume constant driving force merely because acceleration is constant.

types.label: Recalculate acceleration when drive changes but resistance persists
types.summary: A pull doubles, reverses or stops while resistance stays fixed.
checks: Recover the unchanged resistance and rebuild the new resultant.

types.label: Adjust drive to preserve acceleration as resistance increases
types.summary: Acceleration is fixed while resistive force changes.
checks: Keep ma fixed; the drive must change by the resistance change.

types.label: Find immediate acceleration when a support or restraining force is removed
types.summary: A string breaks, a support is removed or a held body is released.
checks: Remove only the vanished force; retain other instantaneous forces and use ΣF = ma.

types.label: Use weight = mass × gravitational field strength
types.summary: Weight, mass or local g is the directly requested quantity.
checks: Use W = mg; distinguish mass from force and use the stated local field.

types.label: Find a scale reading or apparent weight in vertical acceleration
types.summary: A scale, floor or support reports force during vertical acceleration.
checks: Write N − mg = ma with a signed vertical acceleration; the reading is N.
types.boundary_note: Reserve for relating scale readings to acceleration or net force. Identifying which named contact force is measured uses scalemeaning; the gravitational weight itself remains mg. A magnetic-force balance is not an accelerating-lift problem.

types.label: Find cable tension for a vertically accelerating load
types.summary: A lifted load accelerates or decelerates while moving vertically.
checks: Use T − mg = ma; acceleration direction, not velocity direction, sets the sign.

types.label: Explain apparent weightlessness in common free fall
types.summary: A falling or orbiting observer has no support reading despite gravity.
checks: Identify zero contact force and common gravitational acceleration.
types.boundary_note: Orbital explanation may also require D.1.

types.label: Find lift/thrust or acceleration while weight acts
types.summary: A rocket, aircraft or lifted object has upward thrust and downward weight.
checks: Separate thrust from the net force: thrust − weight − resistance = ma.

types.label: Explain mass-independent free-fall acceleration
types.summary: Objects of different masses or weights fall/project freely without drag.
checks: Combine Fg = mg with Fnet = ma and cancel mass; distinguish equal acceleration from equal gravitational force.
types.boundary_note: A.1 trajectory consequences may be used, but the force–mass cancellation is the A.2 content.

types.label: Find the common acceleration of connected bodies
types.summary: Several bodies remain linked and share one acceleration.
checks: Add external forces on the complete system; internal forces cancel; divide by total mass.

types.label: Find a particular tension in a connected chain
types.summary: The requested string force is internal to a multi-body system.
checks: Find common acceleration; isolate the body or group beyond the required string.

types.label: Find the contact force between pushed bodies
types.summary: One object pushes another without a string.
checks: Find system acceleration then use the subsystem accelerated by the contact force.

types.label: Solve two hanging masses over a light smooth pulley
types.summary: Two weights drive a common string acceleration in opposite vertical directions.
checks: Combine the two signed weight–tension equations; then recover tension.

types.label: Solve a table–hanging-mass system
types.summary: One mass moves horizontally and the other vertically.
checks: Use equal acceleration magnitudes along the string and separate normal balance on the table.

types.label: Solve connected bodies involving one or two inclines
types.summary: The connected system includes slope-parallel weight components.
checks: Choose a trial direction; resolve each slope; include friction with a defensible direction.

types.label: Recognise zero tension or a slack connector
types.summary: Both bodies freely fall or the calculated string force would need to push.
checks: Apply the kinematic/force constraints and the condition T ≥ 0; abandon a taut-string model when it fails.

types.label: Couple translating masses to a pulley with rotational inertia
types.summary: A pulley has non-negligible mass or specified moment of inertia, so tensions on the two sides need not be equal.
checks: Write translation equations for the masses and a torque equation for the pulley; link a = αr, or use total translational plus rotational energy.
types.boundary_note: Requires A.4 HL. Do not use the massless-pulley Atwood expression.

types.label: Find maximum common acceleration before an upper block slips
types.summary: Static friction alone accelerates the carried body.
checks: Required friction = mtop a; compare with μs N at that interface.

types.label: Find forces and accelerations when one body slides on another
types.summary: Relative slip occurs and the two bodies need not have equal accelerations.
checks: Put equal-and-opposite kinetic friction on separate diagrams and write two dynamics equations.

types.label: Combine static-friction limits at multiple contacts
types.summary: A stack, tether or multiple rough surfaces offers several possible slip interfaces.
checks: Identify each normal force, calculate the relevant friction limits, and combine them with the separate body/system balances.
types.boundary_note: Distinguish comparing which contact slips first from simultaneous limits; a stationary system does not require finding a common acceleration.

types.label: Identify the direction and role of friction
types.summary: A contact may resist sliding or provide forward/centripetal acceleration.
checks: Identify actual or impending relative motion at that contact; friction opposes that relative slip.
types.boundary_note: Friction need not oppose the object’s velocity.

types.label: Find actual static friction below its limit
types.summary: An object remains at rest or co-moves without slipping.
checks: Use the force balance/dynamics to find the friction demanded; verify Ff ≤ μs N.
types.boundary_note: Do not set Ff = μs N unless at limiting equilibrium.

types.label: Distinguish coefficient from force and compare unchanged contacts
types.summary: The applied force, mass or speed changes but the contact material is unchanged.
checks: Keep the coefficient separate from the force; determine whether N and the friction regime change.

types.label: Distinguish static from kinetic friction at a contact
types.summary: The object may move in the laboratory while remaining at rest relative to its contact.
checks: Decide from relative sliding at the interface, not motion relative to the room.

types.label: Find a breakaway force or decide whether sliding begins
types.summary: An applied force is compared with the largest sustainable static friction.
checks: Find N, calculate μs N and compare with the required tangential force.

types.label: Find the incline angle or coefficient at impending slip
types.summary: A slope is tilted until the body just begins to slide.
checks: Resolve weight; impose mg sin θ = μs mg cos θ at threshold.

types.label: Solve friction when an angled push or pull alters the normal force
types.summary: The driving force also increases or reduces N.
checks: Resolve perpendicular first, then substitute the resulting N into the friction law.

types.label: Recalculate motion after static friction becomes kinetic
types.summary: The object starts moving and μs differs from μd.
checks: Use limiting static friction for the threshold, then μd N for post-breakaway acceleration.

types.label: Find sliding friction, acceleration or coefficient on a level surface
types.summary: The contact is sliding and the kinetic-friction law applies.
checks: Find N and Ff = μd N, then solve the signed resultant equation.

types.label: Solve steady or accelerated sliding on an incline
types.summary: A sliding body experiences a slope weight component and friction.
checks: Use N = mg cos θ when appropriate; combine mg sin θ, μd N and any applied force.

types.label: Infer friction or coefficient from stopping data
types.summary: A body slows over a known time/distance or a speed–time graph.
checks: Recover deceleration or work against friction; infer Ff and then μd.
types.boundary_note: Infer friction from stopping data using dynamics or work-energy. On a slope separate the component of weight; after a hanging load lands, do not retain its previous pulling tension.

types.label: Read static and kinetic coefficients from a force trace
types.summary: A measured force rises to a peak then settles while sliding.
checks: Associate breakaway peak with μs N and sliding plateau with μd N.
types.boundary_note: A graph-reading act is a separate tag, not a separate physics family.

types.label: Compare friction force and deceleration for different masses
types.summary: Bodies on the same level surface have different masses.
checks: Distinguish Ff ∝ m from a = μd g; carry the result into stopping comparisons if required.

types.label: Follow driven motion and subsequent frictional coasting
types.summary: A body is driven for a stated distance or time, then the applied force is removed while friction continues.
checks: Treat the driven and coasting phases separately; propagate the speed or kinetic energy at the changeover; state whether the requested distance is the coasting distance or the total.
types.boundary_note: Either a dynamics/kinematics route or a work–energy route may be valid.

types.label: Find force, extension or spring constant
types.summary: An elastic element is within its stated linear range.
checks: Use F = kx with extension measured from natural length.

types.label: Find spring constant or the linear range from a force–extension graph
types.summary: A graph or paired force/extension values are supplied.
checks: Read the correct gradient orientation and distinguish proportional region from non-linear response.

types.label: Explain the sign and direction of a restoring force
types.summary: The minus sign in F = −kx or the direction away from equilibrium is queried.
checks: Relate force direction to displacement; distinguish extension magnitude from signed displacement.
types.boundary_note: Showing SHM additionally requires the C.1 acceleration criterion.

types.label: Find a static spring extension supporting a load
types.summary: Weight or another steady load is balanced by an elastic force.
checks: Use kx equal to the supported force, not automatically the total weight of an unrelated system.

types.label: Combine forces from two or more springs
types.summary: Several springs act on the same moving or supported body.
checks: Use individual extensions and signed forces, or derive the appropriate effective stiffness.
types.boundary_note: Do not assume every spring has the same extension.

types.label: Find acceleration or maximum force at a specified extension
types.summary: The displacement of a spring-connected mass is given and force/acceleration is asked.
checks: Calculate net elastic and other forces, then use ΣF = ma.
types.boundary_note: A.3 energy or C.1 period data may supply the extension/stiffness.

types.label: Find upthrust from displaced fluid
types.summary: Fluid density and displaced volume are known or recoverable.
checks: Use Fb = ρfluid Vdisplaced g.

types.label: Explain buoyancy as a pressure-resultant force
types.summary: The origin of upthrust or unequal fluid forces is requested.
checks: Use increasing pressure with depth and the resultant upward force over the surface.
types.boundary_note: Hydrostatic pressure knowledge is a cross-topic dependency.

types.label: Relate pressure to a resultant force or supported load
types.summary: Find force from pressure over an area, or infer contact pressure from the load transmitted to a surface.
checks: Use F = pA for uniform pressure, or pressure = supported load / contact area. Establish the load from force balance where needed.
types.boundary_note: Do not describe a solid cylinder pressing on a surface as hydrostatic buoyancy. A stand-alone pressure calculation is a cross-topic bridge, not automatically a full A.2 dynamics problem.

types.label: Find submerged fraction, displaced volume or mean density
types.summary: The object floats or is neutrally buoyant.
checks: Set displaced-fluid weight equal to object weight; use the appropriate total and submerged volumes.

types.label: Find support force or apparent weight in a fluid
types.summary: A scale, string or support acts in addition to buoyancy and weight.
checks: Write the signed vertical equilibrium including all three forces.

types.label: Predict a fluid-level or loading change through displaced weight
types.summary: A floating object melts, takes on a load or moves between fluids.
checks: Compare the fluid displaced before and after using mass/weight conservation and the stated densities.
types.boundary_note: Treat as a derived application rather than a separately memorised rule.

types.label: Find initial rise or fall acceleration in a fluid
types.summary: A held submerged body is released from rest.
checks: At release use buoyancy minus weight and any stated initial drag, then divide by object mass.

types.label: Judge whether buoyancy or weight may be neglected
types.summary: A low-density bubble or dense body is approximated by a reduced force account.
checks: Compare force magnitudes through density/volume ratios before making the approximation.

types.label: Obtain a restoring force from changing immersion
types.summary: A floating body is displaced slightly, changing displaced volume while its weight remains fixed.
checks: Subtract the equilibrium buoyancy; use ΔV = Ax to obtain Fnet = −ρfluid g A x, then identify the restoring acceleration.
types.boundary_note: Proving SHM adds a C.1 demand. Merely quoting an SHM period without a buoyancy step is not this type.

types.label: Calculate Stokes drag or viscosity
types.summary: A small sphere moves through a fluid and the Stokes model is appropriate.
checks: Use Fd = 6πηrv with radius, relative speed and consistent units.

types.label: Scale Stokes drag with size, speed or viscosity
types.summary: Factors change in the linear Stokes drag relation.
checks: Form ratios of ηrv; distinguish radius changes from diameter changes.

types.label: Evaluate a stated linear, quadratic or combined resistance law
types.summary: A force–speed relation is supplied in the question.
checks: Substitute the relative speed and add any separately stated constant resistance.
types.boundary_note: A supplied model is usable; memorising a general quadratic-drag law is not a distinct required A.2 understanding.

types.label: Infer units or dimensions of a drag coefficient
types.summary: The model F = kv or F = kv² is given and the constant’s units are asked.
checks: Rearrange for the coefficient and use force/speed dimensions.
types.boundary_note: Tools-linked derived demand.

types.label: Separate constant and speed-dependent resistance from data
types.summary: Two or more speeds/forces are given for a combined drag model.
checks: Write one equation per measurement and recover the coefficients or components.

types.label: Infer the coefficient in a supplied resistance law
types.summary: A drag model such as F = cv or F = cv² is supplied and c must be inferred from force, terminal-motion or power data.
checks: Find the actual resistive force from the force balance or P/v, then rearrange the stated model; track dimensions separately.
types.boundary_note: Do not assume every quadratic model is Stokes drag; Stokes drag is linear in speed.

types.label: Find a terminal force or speed from zero resultant
types.summary: Steady limiting motion occurs under weight or a driving force and drag.
checks: Set the complete resultant to zero, then use the supplied drag relation.

types.label: Find terminal rise/fall speed with buoyancy and Stokes drag
types.summary: A sphere or bubble reaches terminal motion with three vertical forces.
checks: Use (ρobject − ρfluid)Vg balanced by 6πηrv, with direction handled explicitly.

types.label: Compare terminal speeds when radius, density or viscosity changes
types.summary: A terminal-speed ratio is requested rather than just a drag-force ratio.
checks: Derive the terminal balance first; for a Stokes sphere recover v ∝ r²(ρobject−ρfluid)/η.

types.label: Explain approach to terminal speed
types.summary: The speed rises but acceleration decreases toward zero.
checks: Link increasing drag to decreasing resultant and acceleration; terminal speed is the zero-resultant limit.

types.label: Predict the response to a changed drag or driving condition
types.summary: A parachute opens or mass, drag area or thrust changes during motion.
checks: Find the immediate new resultant at the old speed, then identify the new terminal state.

types.label: Compare forces and acceleration during ascent, apex and descent
types.summary: A projectile reverses its direction while air/fluid resistance acts.
checks: Reverse drag with relative velocity; at the apex distinguish zero speed from zero acceleration.
types.boundary_note: Cross-topic with A.1.

types.label: Describe or sketch slowing under speed-dependent resistance
types.summary: Drive is removed and drag weakens as the body slows.
checks: Use a decreasing deceleration magnitude; infer the curvature of the speed–time graph.

types.label: Relate acceleration or resultant force to speed under drag
types.summary: A graph of acceleration or resultant force against speed is requested for a falling or driven body.
checks: Write ma = driving force − drag(v); use the correct intercept, dependence on v and zero-acceleration terminal-speed intercept.
types.boundary_note: Use only when speed/velocity is the independent variable and acceleration or force is plotted against it. Time-axis graphs belong to dragvt or dragtimeforce; do not assume a linear drag law unless stated.

types.label: Explain coasting or terminal motion under electromagnetic resistance
types.summary: A moving conductor induces a current/force that opposes its motion, or a back emf reduces a driving current as speed increases.
checks: Establish the electromagnetic dependence on speed, then use the net-force/current condition to explain deceleration or the limiting speed.
types.boundary_note: Mixed with D.4. A frictionless powered rod may reach zero current and zero magnetic force, rather than balance two separate fluid forces.

types.label: Explain limitations of a constant-resistance stopping model
types.summary: Why is a calculated stopping distance only an estimate?
checks: Identify an assumption about resistance, brakes or speed dependence that affects the prediction.
types.boundary_note: Do not invent a numerical force calculation where only model limitations are asked.

types.label: Define linear momentum and identify its units/vector nature
types.summary: Momentum itself or its physical classification is requested.
checks: Use p = mv, preserve velocity direction and use kg m s−1.
types.boundary_note: Includes fundamental SI units and dimensions of expressions containing momentum, including units of graph gradients. A dimensional solution need not use E_k = p^2/(2m).

types.label: Calculate or compare momentum from mass and velocity
types.summary: One or more body momenta are needed without an interaction calculation.
checks: Use signed/vector mv; add momenta only for the requested system.

types.label: Resolve or add momentum vectors
types.summary: Motion is non-collinear or a momentum component/vector diagram is requested.
checks: Resolve mv along common axes and sum components before finding magnitude/direction.
types.boundary_note: Quantitative two-dimensional collisions/explosions require HL; a basic vector construction is not automatically a collision.

types.label: Find momentum at a projectile’s highest point
types.summary: The vertical velocity vanishes at an apex but horizontal velocity may persist.
checks: Set only the vertical momentum component to zero.
types.boundary_note: Cross-topic with A.1.

types.label: Relate non-relativistic momentum, mass and kinetic energy
types.summary: Momentum is requested from kinetic energy or equal-momentum bodies are compared.
checks: Use Ek = p²/(2m) or p = √(2mEk), preserving the non-relativistic assumption.
types.boundary_note: Primarily A.3 unless momentum reasoning is assessed; retain as an interface leaf.

types.label: State the momentum-conservation law and its condition
types.summary: A statement of conservation or its external-force condition is required.
checks: State that total system momentum remains constant when resultant external force/impulse is zero.

types.label: Choose a closed system or explain a subsystem’s momentum change
types.summary: A wall, Earth, exhaust or thrown object may lie outside the chosen system.
checks: Identify momentum transfer across the boundary; enlarge the system or include external impulse.

types.label: Derive two-body momentum conservation from Newton’s laws
types.summary: The conservation equation must be justified rather than merely used.
checks: Use equal-and-opposite interaction forces over the same time and convert impulses to momentum changes.

types.label: Conserve one momentum component despite a force in another direction
types.summary: An external force or launch impulse acts vertically while horizontal momentum remains unchanged, or vice versa.
checks: Choose axes and apply the no-external-impulse condition to the relevant component only.
types.boundary_note: A whole-system vector conservation claim can be false when only one component is conserved.

types.label: Identify resultant force as rate of momentum change
types.summary: The momentum form of Newton’s second law or a nonzero-force consequence is central.
checks: Use Fnet = Δp/Δt; a changing direction also changes the momentum vector.

types.label: State when the momentum law reduces to F = ma
types.summary: The distinction between the two forms of Newton’s second law is asked.
checks: Make the constant-mass condition explicit for the stated system.

types.label: Define impulse and connect it to momentum change
types.summary: Impulse’s definition, unit or equivalent expression is requested.
checks: State J = Faverage Δt = Δp with the appropriate resultant-force condition.

types.label: Find impulse for a straight-line speed change
types.summary: The object speeds up, stops or launches without a reversal.
checks: Use J = m(v−u) with a sign convention and convert units.

types.label: Find impulse when the object reverses direction
types.summary: Incoming and outgoing velocities point oppositely.
checks: Assign opposite signs before subtraction; do not subtract speed magnitudes.

types.label: Find impulse in an oblique rebound
types.summary: An impact reverses or changes the velocity component normal to a surface while the tangential component is unchanged.
checks: Resolve the initial and final momenta and subtract; for a smooth elastic wall only the normal component reverses.
types.boundary_note: Current quantitative 2D collision scope is HL. A qualitative direction argument is separately usable at SL.

types.label: Relate impulse on a surface to impulse on the object
types.summary: The required impulse belongs to the wall, Earth or striking body’s partner.
checks: Find one body’s momentum change and reverse the impulse using the interaction pair.

types.label: Calculate impulse from a stated force and duration
types.summary: The force and its duration are supplied numerically or symbolically, without a graph.
checks: Use J = Faverage Δt, distinguishing impulse from the force and keeping the force direction.

types.label: Find vector momentum change over a curved path
types.summary: An object turns through a known angle while its speed may remain constant; no impact is required.
checks: Subtract final and initial momentum vectors; for equal magnitudes use the chord of the momentum-vector diagram.
types.boundary_note: Includes the change of a requested momentum component over a curved path. A quarter-turn on a string is not an oblique collision and should not inherit the HL-only two-dimensional-collision condition.
types.level_scope: SL+HL: vector/component momentum change; not a quantitative two-dimensional collision

types.label: Find average net force or duration from momentum change
types.summary: A contact interval and pre/post velocities, or force and impulse, are supplied.
checks: Compute the complete momentum change and use Faverage = Δp/Δt.

types.label: Find average contact force when weight also acts during impact
types.summary: A landing, catch or vertical stop asks for ground/hand/rope force rather than net force.
checks: Calculate net average force from impulse, then add/subtract weight using a signed force balance.

types.label: Explain reduced impact force by increasing stopping time
types.summary: Padding, bending knees or a longer interaction changes duration for a fixed momentum change.
checks: Keep Δp fixed and compare mean force through Δp/Δt.
types.boundary_note: Do not claim a longer time necessarily changes impulse.

types.label: Find impulse or impact force using energy-derived speeds
types.summary: A drop height, launch height or rebound height supplies a speed needed in a momentum-change calculation.
checks: Use energy conservation to obtain the relevant speed(s), assign velocity signs, then calculate impulse or average force.
types.boundary_note: A.3/A.1 cross-topic route.

types.label: Explain increased outgoing momentum from prolonged driving contact
types.summary: A racket, club or other driver remains in contact longer and the question asks why the outgoing speed rises.
checks: Compare impulse as force integrated over time; a larger area produces a larger momentum change.
types.boundary_note: Unlike cushioning, the momentum change is not fixed. Longer contact alone does not guarantee a larger impulse if the force changes compensatingly.

types.label: Find impulse from signed area under a force–time graph
types.summary: The force history is shown graphically.
checks: Add geometric signed areas or an appropriate numerical area estimate.

types.label: Infer an unknown pulse height or duration from its impulse
types.summary: The graph shape and momentum change constrain an unknown graph dimension.
checks: Equate the pulse area to Δp and solve for the peak or time.

types.label: Find later velocity or maximum speed from a force history
types.summary: A force pulse/history acts on an initially moving or stationary body.
checks: Use accumulated signed impulse: p(t) = p0 + area; divide by mass and inspect extrema.

types.label: Find resultant force from a momentum–time graph
types.summary: Momentum is plotted against time and force is requested.
checks: Use the local/interval slope with the correct sign and units.

types.label: Translate a force history into a momentum-time graph or vice versa
types.summary: The required answer is the shape of the other force/momentum representation.
checks: Use force as momentum slope and impulse as momentum change interval by interval.

types.label: Carry one or more impulses into a kinetic-energy result
types.summary: Repeated force pulses or impulse comparisons lead to an energy question.
checks: Accumulate signed momentum, then use Ek = p²/(2m).
types.boundary_note: A.3 cross-topic; impulses add linearly, kinetic energies do not.

types.label: Find an unknown velocity or mass when bodies separate after collision
types.summary: One-dimensional before/after data give all but one momentum quantity.
checks: Use signed total momentum before = after; apply the supplied collision information.
types.boundary_note: Does not require solving momentum and kinetic energy simultaneously.

types.label: Find common speed when a moving body sticks to a stationary target
types.summary: The bodies join and one is initially at rest.
checks: Use m1u1 = (m1+m2)v.

types.label: Solve a sticking collision with two initially moving bodies
types.summary: Both initial momenta are nonzero, possibly opposite.
checks: Add signed initial momenta and divide by combined mass.

types.label: Test proposed outcomes using conservation constraints
types.summary: Several possible after-collision states or velocity graphs are offered.
checks: Check total signed momentum; impose any stated energy/collision constraint separately.

types.label: Distinguish elastic and inelastic collisions conceptually
types.summary: Conserved quantities or the meaning of elastic/inelastic is asked.
checks: Momentum is conserved for the isolated system; total kinetic energy is additionally conserved only in elastic collisions.

types.label: Test elasticity by comparing total kinetic energies
types.summary: Before/after velocities and masses allow a quantitative energy check.
checks: Calculate total initial and final kinetic energies and compare, not just individual speeds.

types.label: Find kinetic energy lost, retained or transformed in a collision
types.summary: A difference, fraction or destination of collision energy is asked.
checks: Compute system kinetic energies before and after; interpret any loss as transfer to other forms.

types.label: Connect a collision to a later climb, stop or motion stage
types.summary: Momentum conservation applies during a brief impact, followed by a distinct energy/force stage.
checks: Separate stages and laws; carry the immediate post-collision speed into the later stage.
types.boundary_note: A.1/A.3 cross-topic; never conserve mechanical energy across an inelastic impact.

types.label: Solve a general elastic collision using simultaneous momentum and energy equations
types.summary: Two unknown final speeds require the full coupled conservation solution.
checks: Solve both system conservation equations with the nontrivial collision branch.
types.boundary_note: Explicitly not required by current guidance; retain as historical/extension evidence.

types.label: Test or justify the equal-mass velocity-exchange outcome
types.summary: A particular equal-mass elastic outcome is proposed or must be checked.
checks: Verify both momentum and kinetic energy for the proposed exchange; distinguish a check from the general two-unknown solver.
types.boundary_note: A demand to solve the general simultaneous momentum/energy equations belongs to the separate not-required extension.

types.label: Find the kinetic energy transferred from one colliding body
types.summary: A projectile loses kinetic energy while the other body gains it; the whole collision may still be elastic.
checks: Compare that body’s own initial and final kinetic energies, not the total system loss; distinguish transfer from dissipation.
types.boundary_note: Nuclear moderation can supply the context without changing the classical calculation.

types.label: Follow repeated fractional energy transfer in collisions
types.summary: Each collision removes a fixed fraction of the projectile’s remaining energy.
checks: Apply the remaining-energy factor successively, or E_n = E_0 q^n; explain why the absolute loss shrinks.
types.boundary_note: Usually mixed with nuclear moderation; logarithmic counting is not itself an A.2 force calculation.

types.label: Infer a post-collision speed from a stated energy-retention fraction
types.summary: The collision loses a specified fraction of total kinetic energy and symmetry or the stated final motion fixes the mass/speed relationship.
checks: Set Kfinal = f Kinitial and solve for the final speed; use momentum only if independently needed.
types.boundary_note: Do not confuse this with using the subsequent pendulum rise to find speed: the latter is A.3 alone.

types.label: Explain where kinetic energy goes in an inelastic collision
types.summary: The question asks why kinetic energy decreases or asks for energy transformations during impact.
checks: Identify transfer to internal energy, deformation, sound or other relevant stores; total energy is conserved even when the translational kinetic energy is not.
types.boundary_note: Do not tag a subsequent stand-alone calculation of kinetic energy from an already known speed as momentum conservation.

types.label: Find an unknown outgoing momentum vector in a two-dimensional collision
types.summary: A collision has non-collinear paths and one vector is unknown.
checks: Conserve momentum independently in x and y, then reconstruct speed/direction.

types.label: Find common speed and direction after a two-dimensional sticking collision
types.summary: Bodies approach non-collinearly and join.
checks: Add the incoming momentum vectors and divide by total mass.

types.label: Find recoil or fragment motion from zero initial momentum
types.summary: A stationary system, or zero-total-momentum system, separates.
checks: Require equal-and-opposite total fragment momenta with their actual masses.

types.label: Solve separation from a moving system
types.summary: The parent body or projectile has nonzero momentum before separation.
checks: Retain the parent’s initial momentum; write all velocities in the same frame.

types.label: Solve recoil when ejection speed is relative to the launcher
types.summary: A jump, throw or shot is specified relative to the recoiling body.
checks: Convert the velocity constraint to one inertial frame before conserving momentum.
types.boundary_note: Cross-topic with A.5 velocity addition when explicitly required.

types.label: Reconstruct a two-dimensional explosion or missing fragment vector
types.summary: Fragment directions are non-collinear.
checks: Subtract known final momenta from initial total momentum component by component.

types.label: Use an internal spring release and recoil energy
types.summary: A spring or internal energy store separates bodies initially at rest.
checks: Use momentum to relate velocities and the released energy to determine their magnitudes.
types.boundary_note: Energy source may require A.3; retain any provided scaffold.

types.label: Compare kinetic energies of recoiling fragments
types.summary: Fragments have equal-and-opposite momentum but different masses.
checks: Use Ek = p²/(2m); the lighter fragment has the larger kinetic energy.

types.label: Explain or calculate kinetic-energy gain in an explosion
types.summary: Momentum remains conserved while kinetic energy increases.
checks: Identify internal energy converted to kinetic energy and compare before/after totals.

types.label: Infer an unseen product or reject a single-product process
types.summary: Observed products cannot account for the initial total momentum.
checks: Use the momentum shortfall to identify a required additional carrier or direction.
types.boundary_note: Nuclear/photon/relativistic detail is separately tagged; do not make it all core A.2.

types.label: Find thrust from exhaust mass flow and relative speed
types.summary: Material is expelled at a stated rate and speed.
checks: Find the rate of momentum transferred to the exhaust in the stated frame/model.

types.label: Find acceleration after separating thrust, weight and changing mass
types.summary: Thrust is supplied or derived and the vehicle’s current mass is specified.
checks: Use thrust minus external opposing forces, divided by the instantaneous vehicle mass.

types.label: Explain increasing acceleration or delayed lift-off as fuel is used
types.summary: Thrust is sustained while mass/weight falls.
checks: Track both the force balance and the decreasing mass; identify the lift-off condition.

types.label: Explain propeller, fan, rotor or rocket propulsion
types.summary: A qualitative account of pushing fluid/exhaust is needed.
checks: Describe momentum given to the flow and the opposite force on the propulsion system.
types.boundary_note: No external material is needed for a rocket in vacuum.

types.label: Find force from a stream brought to rest
types.summary: Particles, water or other matter arrive with mass per unit time and velocity.
checks: Use force = mass flow rate × signed velocity change.

types.label: Find force when a stream rebounds or changes direction
types.summary: The outgoing stream still has momentum, often reversed or angled.
checks: Use the full incoming-to-outgoing vector momentum change per unit time.

types.label: Find a scale/support reading while material accumulates
types.summary: Incoming material adds both an impact momentum flux and accumulated weight.
checks: Add the momentum-transfer force to the weight of material already supported.

types.label: Find force needed to load or accelerate matter onto a moving carrier
types.summary: Material joins a belt, cart or carrier with a different initial velocity.
checks: Find the material’s momentum gain per unit time and the opposing force on the carrier.

types.label: Derive drag from the mass swept up each second
types.summary: Density, cross-sectional area and speed determine intercepted material.
checks: Use dm/dt = ρAv, then multiply by the specified velocity change.
types.boundary_note: Derived model; assumptions must be stated rather than treating F ∝ v² as universal.

types.label: Compare momentum-flow force with energy-flow power
types.summary: A stream exerts a force and transfers kinetic energy per unit time.
checks: Keep momentum rate and energy rate distinct; use the same incoming/outgoing flow model.
types.boundary_note: A.3 cross-topic.

types.label: Explain a macroscopic force through repeated microscopic momentum changes
types.summary: Molecules or photons repeatedly collide with a boundary.
checks: Combine impulse per event with event rate and identify the reaction on the boundary.
types.boundary_note: Gas-pressure and radiation/photon formulas belong to B.3/E.2 and are not automatically core A.2.

types.label: Obtain force or pressure from photon momentum flux
types.summary: Light is absorbed or reflected and the force/pressure must be derived from transferred momentum per unit time.
checks: Use the supplied or E.2 photon momentum, count incident photons, apply the absorption/reflection momentum change, then F = Δp/Δt and P = F/A if needed.
types.boundary_note: Never use p = mv for a photon. Photon properties are E.2; the momentum-rate force step is the A.2 contribution.

types.label: Convert period, frequency or angular speed to linear speed
types.summary: A radius and revolution rate/period describe a circular path.
checks: Use v = 2πr/T = 2πrf = ωr; convert revolution units.

types.label: Compare points at different radii on a common rotating body
types.summary: Points share angular speed/period but not linear speed or radial acceleration.
checks: Hold ω fixed; use v = ωr and a = ω²r.

types.label: Find centripetal acceleration, radius or required speed
types.summary: The circular kinematic requirement is the target, without a separate real-force balance.
checks: Use a = v²/r = ω²r = 4π²r/T² in the convenient form.

types.label: Find the inward resultant required by circular motion
types.summary: Mass and circular-motion data determine the net inward force.
checks: Use Fnet,radial = mv²/r; do not call this automatically a particular tension or support force.

types.label: Scale circular force or acceleration when variables change
types.summary: The requested answer is a factor/ratio under changed speed, radius, mass or energy.
checks: Choose the form consistent with what is held fixed before forming the ratio.

types.label: Resolve circular-motion components at a given time or phase
types.summary: A point on a rotating body has known angular speed and initial phase; one Cartesian component is requested later.
checks: Advance the phase by ωt, place the tangent correctly and resolve the position or velocity into the requested component.
types.boundary_note: Projection may also be expressed as SHM (C.1). This is not the excluded non-uniform vertical force analysis at arbitrary angles.

types.label: Identify tangential velocity and inward acceleration/resultant
types.summary: A diagram or statement asks for the directions in uniform circular motion.
checks: Velocity is tangent; acceleration and net force point inward for uniform circular motion.
types.boundary_note: In non-uniform motion there may also be tangential acceleration.

types.label: Explain acceleration at constant speed
types.summary: The body moves at constant speed but the velocity direction changes.
checks: Explain the changing velocity vector and nonzero inward acceleration/resultant.

types.label: Explain why an inward perpendicular force does no work
types.summary: The question connects centripetal force with energy or work.
checks: Use zero force component along instantaneous displacement; distinguish this force from any tangential force.
types.boundary_note: Do not infer that every force on every circular path does no work; A.3 cross-link.

types.label: Predict motion immediately after a circular constraint disappears
types.summary: A string breaks or an inward constraint is removed.
checks: Use the instantaneous tangential velocity; then apply the remaining real forces.
types.boundary_note: Subsequent projectile or field motion need not be a straight line.

types.label: Explain apparent outward motion in a turning vehicle
types.summary: A passenger appears to be pushed outward during a turn.
checks: Describe the inertia/insufficient inward force in an inertial frame and the contact forces actually acting.

types.label: Construct the change in velocity in circular motion
types.summary: Equal-speed tangential velocity vectors at two points must be subtracted.
checks: Place the velocity vectors tail-to-tail or add the negative initial vector; identify Δv and its limiting inward direction.
types.boundary_note: The vector operation also uses Tools/A.1; do not label this as a two-dimensional collision.

types.label: Identify the real interaction supplying the inward resultant
types.summary: The question asks what causes circular motion, rather than asking for a numerical centripetal force.
checks: Name the actual interaction, such as friction, tension, gravity or a contact force; do not add centripetal force as a further interaction.
types.boundary_note: Use a setup-specific leaf as well only when that setup’s force balance is actually assessed.

types.label: Distinguish radial and tangential acceleration in non-uniform circular motion
types.summary: The question asks whether the resultant can vanish in a pendulum or other changing-speed circular motion.
checks: A speed change requires tangential acceleration; turning requires radial acceleration v^2/r. In a moving pendulum these components vanish at different positions, so its resultant need not vanish at equilibrium.
types.boundary_note: Qualitative distinction is current. Quantitative non-uniform vertical-circle force analysis away from the top and bottom is not required.

types.label: Find maximum speed on a flat circular road
types.summary: Tyre friction supplies the inward resultant and has a maximum.
checks: Set mv²/r ≤ μs N with N = mg when vertical balance applies.

types.label: Find the slip limit of an object on a rotating disc
types.summary: Static friction makes a body co-rotate with a platform.
checks: Compare mω²r with μs N to determine maximum rate/radius or first slip.

types.label: Solve a conical-pendulum geometry
types.summary: The string is inclined while the mass moves in a horizontal circle.
checks: Resolve T vertically and radially; use the actual horizontal radius, not string length.
types.boundary_note: Conical pendulums are distinct from the excluded quantitative banked-surface problems.

types.label: Test whether a proposed horizontal circular path is possible
types.summary: A suggested string or force arrangement may omit support against gravity.
checks: Demand both vertical equilibrium and an inward resultant; reject a missing-force model.

types.label: Use a hanging counterweight to set circular-motion tension
types.summary: A rotating mass and hanging mass share an ideal string or tube.
checks: Use the hanging mass’s condition to obtain tension and apply the radial equation to the rotating mass.

types.label: Spring provides a horizontal centripetal force
types.summary: A rotating mass stretches a spring and the extension, radius, spring constant or speed is sought.
checks: Distinguish natural length, extension and orbital radius; equate kx to mv²/r and solve.
types.boundary_note: Circular equilibrium of a spring is A.2; an oscillation-period question is C.1.

types.label: Explain the force picture or effect of banking qualitatively
types.summary: A banked road or surface changes how contact forces provide inward force.
checks: Resolve conceptually: the contact-force components support weight and supply radial acceleration.
types.boundary_note: Keep qualitative banked-surface reasoning separate from a quantitative banked-track limit.

types.label: Calculate a speed/angle limit on a banked surface
types.summary: Numerical/algebraic banking geometry, with or without tyre friction, must be solved.
checks: Resolve normal/friction forces into radial and vertical components and impose the relevant limit.
types.boundary_note: Quantitative treatment of banked surfaces is explicitly not required.

types.label: Derive the no-slip speed or angular-speed condition
types.summary: Derive the minimum speed needed to prevent a rider sliding down a rotating wall.
checks: Vertically f_s = mg; radially N = mv²/R = mω²R; require f_s ≤ μ_s N. Thus ω_min = √(g/(μ_s R)).
types.boundary_note: Normal reaction supplies the inward force. Friction acts vertically, not radially. A supplied threshold formula removes the need to repeat its derivation.

types.label: Find circular speed using a normal force already obtained
types.summary: Previous part supplies the radial normal force.
checks: Use N = mv²/R to find v, taking the earlier N as given.
types.boundary_note: Do not count the previous friction derivation again as an operational prerequisite.

types.label: Find the minimum normal force from the vertical no-slip condition
types.summary: Find the minimum horizontal reaction before calculating any circular speed.
checks: Use f_s = mg and f_s ≤ μ_s N to obtain N_min = mg/μ_s.
types.boundary_note: This part does not itself require mv²/R.

types.label: Test no-slip using a supplied minimum-speed expression
types.summary: The preceding part supplies ω_min; compare it with a stated rotation rate.
checks: Substitute in the supplied expression, convert rpm to rad s⁻¹, compare.
types.boundary_note: A fresh force-balance derivation is an alternative route, not necessary to answer this part.

types.label: Find tension or support at the top of a vertical circle
types.summary: The body is at the highest point and the inward direction is downward.
checks: Construct the inward resultant from the actual contact geometry; often T + mg = mv²/r.
types.boundary_note: The sign of the support force depends on the physical side of the track.

types.label: Find tension or support at the bottom of a vertical circle
types.summary: The body is at the lowest point and the inward direction is upward.
checks: For an inner constraint use T or N minus mg = mv²/r.

types.label: Compare top and bottom tension/support or identify its extrema
types.summary: A vertical path’s constraint force is compared at different heights.
checks: Use the correct radial equations and, for non-uniform motion, the changing speed.

types.label: Find loss of contact at a crest or outer curved surface
types.summary: A body passes over a crest and the normal force can drop to zero.
checks: Use mg − N = mv²/r at the top of a convex crest; impose N = 0 at loss of contact.

types.label: Find minimum top speed for a string to remain taut or inner contact to persist
types.summary: At the top, the constraint force approaches its lowest allowed value.
checks: Set the limiting tension/normal to zero in the correct radial equation.

types.label: Find minimum launch speed or height for completing a vertical loop
types.summary: The limiting top condition must be connected to a lower point by energy.
checks: Use the top contact condition, then an appropriate energy balance between heights.
types.boundary_note: Cross-topic with A.3; state the friction/energy assumptions.

types.label: Resolve forces at other angles in a non-uniform vertical circle
types.summary: The required force analysis occurs away from top or bottom and speed changes.
checks: Resolve radial and tangential force components for the actual angle.
types.boundary_note: Explicitly not required by current guidance; do not discard top/bottom sibling parts.

types.label: Resolve forces at a side or other angle in an explicitly uniform vertical circle
types.summary: Constant speed is explicitly maintained and the radial force is requested away from the top or bottom.
checks: Project real forces onto the inward radial direction and set their resultant equal to mv²/r.
types.boundary_note: Do not transfer this automatically to a non-uniform vertical circle: current guidance does not require off-top/bottom force analysis for that case. A rigid rod is not an ideal string: its force need not be along the rod. For a requested force arrow/scale diagram, use the diagram-demand leaf instead of a quantitative radial-balance leaf.

types.label: Identify which field force acts on the body
types.summary: The demand is to identify gravitational, electric or magnetic interaction rather than map the field.
checks: Use the charge/current/motion information to name the actual force.
types.boundary_note: Pure field direction/magnitude questions retain their primary D.2/D.3 home.

types.label: Use an electric force in equilibrium or linear dynamics
types.summary: An electric force must be combined with weight, tension or ΣF = ma.
checks: Obtain the field force from the relevant D-topic relation, then solve the mechanical balance.
types.boundary_note: Mixed with D.2/D.3; formula recall alone is not direct A.2.

types.label: Use a magnetic force in an equilibrium or acceleration balance
types.summary: A magnetic force supports weight or combines with other forces.
checks: Obtain the magnetic force and use the required balance/dynamics equation.
types.boundary_note: Mixed with D.3; pure hand-rule questions are not direct A.2.

types.label: Find the magnitude or direction of an electric force
types.summary: A charge and electric field or electrostatic interaction are supplied.
checks: Use the field-specific force relation and the charge sign to obtain the vector force.
types.boundary_note: Primary field knowledge is D.2/D.3; retain as a mixed force-interface demand, not a pure A.2 census item.

types.label: Find the magnetic force on a moving charge
types.summary: A moving charge and magnetic field define a Lorentz-force magnitude or direction.
checks: Use |q|vB sin θ and the cross-product/right-hand direction, reversing for negative charge.
types.boundary_note: Primary D.3 knowledge; mixed force-interface demand.

types.label: Find the magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor
types.summary: Current, wire length and field determine a force or its direction.
checks: Use BIL sin θ and the field/current orientation.
types.boundary_note: Primary D.3 knowledge; mixed force-interface demand.

types.label: Predict a deflected path in a non-uniform electric field
types.summary: A charged projectile passes near another charge or a nucleus and its curvature or deflection is requested.
checks: Identify attractive or repulsive force and how it changes with separation; connect the local force to the change in velocity.
types.boundary_note: Primarily D.2/E.1 knowledge with an A.2 dynamics component; not uniform circular motion.

types.label: Balance crossed electric and magnetic forces
types.summary: A charged particle passes undeflected through perpendicular electric and magnetic fields.
checks: Set the opposing electric and magnetic forces equal; use qE = qvB and confirm the directions for the particle’s sign.
types.boundary_note: The field relations are D.3 knowledge; this is a mixed force-balance task.

types.label: Test electric-force equilibrium after a small displacement
types.summary: A charge starts at a zero-resultant point and is displaced along or across an axis.
checks: Compare the changed force components; a restoring force indicates local stability, while a force away from equilibrium indicates instability.
types.boundary_note: The equilibrium may be stable in one direction but unstable in another; the field setup belongs to D.2.

types.label: Identify or calculate the force/acceleration providing an orbit
types.summary: The assessed point is the inward gravitational resultant on an orbiting body.
checks: Distinguish gravitational force from an additional centripetal interaction; use the circular requirement if needed.
types.boundary_note: D.1 cross-topic when inverse-square field knowledge is required.

types.label: Find orbital speed, period or central mass by radial balance
types.summary: The inverse-square gravitational relation must be equated to the circular-motion requirement.
checks: Use GMm/r² = mv²/r and the period relation; measure r from the central body’s centre.
types.boundary_note: Mixed with D.1.

types.label: Compare circular orbits using gravitational radial balance
types.summary: Orbit radius, central mass or orbiting mass changes.
checks: Derive the relevant r/M dependence before taking ratios; distinguish force from acceleration.
types.boundary_note: Mixed with D.1.

types.label: Explain orbital change when atmospheric drag acts
types.summary: A satellite experiences resistance and its orbital radius and speed change.
checks: Distinguish drag’s immediate tangential effect from the speed of a later lower orbit; combine mechanical-energy loss with orbital relations.
types.boundary_note: A mixed D.1/A.3 extension; not evidence of a Stokes-law calculation.

types.label: Explain speed or kinetic-energy change in a non-circular orbit
types.summary: Gravity is not always perpendicular to velocity in an elliptical or otherwise non-circular trajectory.
checks: Identify the tangential force component or the exchange between gravitational potential and kinetic energies; contrast this with uniform circular motion.
types.boundary_note: Mixed with D.1/A.3; the no-work conclusion applies to perpendicular force, not all orbital motion.

types.label: Find the spin limit for contact with a rotating planet or asteroid
types.summary: An object rests on the outside surface of a rotating gravitating body and contact or apparent weight is tested.
checks: Write mg−N=mω²r at the equator, require N≥0 and use N=0 at the limiting angular speed; substitute the gravitational field model only when needed.
types.boundary_note: This is a maximum surface-spin/contact condition, not the minimum speed at the top of an inside loop.

types.label: Find radius, field, momentum or period of a magnetic circular path
types.summary: A moving charge’s magnetic force supplies the radial resultant.
checks: Use |q|vB = mv²/r for perpendicular motion; combine with the relevant momentum/period relation.
types.boundary_note: Mixed with D.3; relativistic momentum requires a separate eligibility check.

types.label: Explain circular magnetic steering without a speed change
types.summary: The magnetic force remains perpendicular to velocity.
checks: Explain direction change, no work and the conditions for a circular rather than helical path.
types.boundary_note: Mixed with D.3.

types.label: Use electrostatic attraction as a centripetal force
types.summary: Coulomb attraction supplies the inward force in an orbital model.
checks: Equate the Coulomb force to mv²/r and solve within the supplied model.
types.boundary_note: Mixed with D.2/D.3/E.1; distinguish a model calculation from a required atomic derivation.

types.label: Track curvature as magnetic field or particle speed changes
types.summary: A particle follows a non-circular path because B varies spatially or its momentum changes through another process.
checks: Use the instantaneous radius of curvature r = p/(|q|B); distinguish field variation from actual loss of kinetic energy.
types.boundary_note: A changing local curvature does not mean the magnetic force itself does work.

types.label: Choose or interpret a linearised force–acceleration experiment
types.summary: Force, acceleration or total moving mass are varied systematically; suitable axes or a gradient are requested.
checks: Use Fnet = ma to choose Fnet against a at fixed mass, or a against 1/m at fixed resultant; interpret the gradient with the actual controlled variables.
types.boundary_note: Distinct from circular-force linearisation. Generic best-fit lines or uncertainty calculations alone belong to Tools.

types.label: Linearise or test a supplied drag model
types.summary: Data are to distinguish or fit a stated drag dependence.
checks: Rearrange the physical model into a straight-line form and interpret slope/intercept.
types.boundary_note: Tools-linked; supplied quadratic models do not create a new required formula.

types.label: Explain a mechanics-specific experimental bias or improvement
types.summary: The error changes an identified force, radius, timing or model assumption.
checks: Trace how the physical change biases the inferred mechanics quantity.
types.boundary_note: Do not include context-only generic uncertainty, control-variable or graphing tasks.

types.label: Linearise or interpret circular-motion data
types.summary: A graph relates centripetal acceleration or force to radius, period, frequency or speed.
checks: Derive the proportionality from a = 4π²r/T² or F = mv²/r before choosing axes or interpreting a gradient.
types.boundary_note: Tools are used, but the particular circular-motion model is essential.

types.label: Infer horizontal acceleration from the tilt of an unknown support force
types.summary: A suspended mass or tilted rotor/thrust system has zero vertical acceleration; its support-force magnitude is not supplied.
checks: Resolve the single oblique support force: vertical component balances weight; divide horizontal and vertical equations to obtain a = g tan(theta) for tilt from vertical.
types.boundary_note: Distinct from resolving a known applied force, and from a conical pendulum: straight-line acceleration is possible and no circular-motion equation is required.

types.label: Identify the contact force measured by a scale
types.summary: The question asks what a weighing scale reads in terms of named forces, rather than calculating the force from acceleration.
checks: Identify the normal/contact force acting between the person and the scale; the scale measures that interaction, not the resultant on the person.
types.boundary_note: R, mg and R-mg are distinct. Merely identifying R does not require solving F = ma. A scale calibrated in mass units reports an inferred mass from force.

types.label: Compare upthrust using displaced-volume and fluid-density ratios
types.summary: Immersed bodies differ in radius, volume or material density; the demand is a ratio of buoyant forces.
checks: Use F_b = rho_fluid V_displaced g. For similarly shaped, fully submerged spheres in the same fluid, F_b is proportional to radius cubed.
types.boundary_note: Object density is not fluid density. This is not a test of whether buoyancy or weight can be neglected.

types.label: Sketch velocity or speed against time when resistance acts
types.summary: The horizontal axis is time and the requested vertical axis is velocity or speed, during ascent, descent or a change of medium.
checks: Use the sign and size of the resultant to infer the gradient of velocity-time; track initial conditions, turning points and terminal motion.
types.boundary_note: Do not substitute an acceleration-speed graph or a force-time graph. Signed velocity may cross zero; speed cannot.

types.label: Sketch acceleration or resultant force against time under resistance
types.summary: The question asks for a(t) or resultant F(t), often using a supplied velocity-time graph for a falling body.
checks: Read how the velocity-time gradient changes; use F_net = ma. For release from rest with negligible initial drag, resultant starts at weight and tends towards zero at terminal speed.
types.boundary_note: Time is the horizontal variable. A graph of acceleration against speed is a different demand; force due to drag is not the same as resultant force.

types.label: Sketch velocity or speed during contact from a force history
types.summary: A force-time pulse is given and the requested output is a velocity-time or speed-time curve during the interaction.
checks: Use F/m as the local velocity-time gradient and the initial velocity to construct the curve; equivalently accumulate impulse and divide by mass.
types.boundary_note: Keep the requested variable explicit: p(t), v(t) and speed(t) are not interchangeable labels. The reviewed tennis example starts from rest and speeds up; it is not a rebound.

types.label: Scale a jet or thrust force when the flow rate changes
types.summary: A nozzle or hose has fixed area and a changed volumetric or mass flow rate; infer the force ratio.
checks: Combine F = mass_flow_rate times speed with volume_flow_rate = A v. At fixed fluid density and outlet area, force is proportional to the square of volume flow rate.
types.boundary_note: This is outgoing-jet momentum flow, not drag due to sweeping material out of the way. Distinguish fixed area from fixed outlet speed.
